entities.summary: Martín de Azpilcueta, or Doctor Navarrus, was a Navarrese canonist, theologian and economist who lived from unknown to 1586-06-01. He was born in Navarre, Spain, and studied at the University of Navarre. His most notable work is the 'Comentario a las Siete Partidas', a comprehensive commentary on the legal code of Alfonso X of Castile, which became a cornerstone of canon law in the 16th century. He also contributed to the development of modern economics, particularly in the field of monetary theory. Azpilcueta's work had a significant impact on the Catholic Church and the Spanish monarchy, and his ideas influenced many notable thinkers of his time, including Philip II of Spain and Francisco de Vitoria. The 'Comentario' remains an important source for understanding the evolution of canon law and the development of modern economics. Azpilcueta's legacy also extends to the field of theology, where his work on the relationship between law and religion continues to be studied by scholars today. His writings on the subject have been widely praised for their clarity and depth, and he is still considered one of the most important theologians of the 16th century. In 2001, Azpilcueta was named a Doctor of the Church by Pope John Paul II, a testament to his enduring influence on the Catholic Church.

Martín de Azpilcueta, also known as Doctor Navarrus, was a Navarrese canonist, theologian, and economist born on December 22, 1492, in Barásoain, Navarre, Spain. He studied at the University of Navarre and later at the University of Alcalá, where he earned his doctorate in canon law. Azpilcueta's work had a significant impact on the development of Spanish law and the Catholic Church's understanding of property rights.

As a key figure in the Spanish Inquisition, he contributed to the drafting of the 1526 Alumbrados laws, which aimed to counter heresy and promote orthodoxy. His economic theories, as outlined in his book 'Commentary on the Law of God,' influenced the development of Spanish mercantilism and the country's economic policies.

Azpilcueta's legacy extends to the modern era, with his ideas on property rights and the role of the state in regulating economic activity continuing to shape contemporary debates in economics and law. His work also had a lasting impact on the Catholic Church, with his writings on canon law and theology remaining influential among scholars to this day.

A testament to his enduring influence, Azpilcueta's name is still invoked by scholars and policymakers today, serving as a reminder of the profound impact of his ideas on the course of modern history.
